_note: Batch 10 — the final 113. Guitars, piano, organ, Rhodes, synth lead, pads, strings, horns and the mix bus. This completes the bank at 713 of 713.

questions.q: How do I make my distorted guitar sound bigger?
questions.short: Two performances hard-panned. One guitar widened is not bigger, it is phasey.
steps: Record the part twice and pan the takes 100% left and right.
Use a different amp, cabinet or pickup on each so they differ in tone as well as timing.
Reduce the gain on both; high gain sounds huge soloed and small in a mix.
High-pass both at 100 Hz so the bass keeps the bottom.
Add a short room reverb to both from the same send.
questions.why: Size in guitars is width, and width requires two genuinely different signals. Less gain also makes them bigger in context, because high-gain distortion is itself a compressor and removes the dynamic range that reads as power.
questions.watch: Two takes with identical tone fuse into one and sound narrower than a single track.

questions.q: How do I tighten up my distorted guitar?
questions.short: Less gain and a higher high-pass. Looseness is low-end mush, not timing.
steps: Reduce the amp's gain. This is the single biggest change.
High-pass at 100–150 Hz.
Cut 3 dB at 200–400 Hz where high-gain amps pile up.
Tighten the palm-muted sections with light compression, 3:1 at 2 dB.
Align the two doubled takes' attacks if they are flamming.
questions.why: High-gain distortion generates enormous low-mid energy that sustains far longer than the note, which is heard as looseness. Reducing gain at the amp is the only move that addresses the cause rather than the symptom.
questions.watch: Less gain always feels wrong when soloed and right in the mix. Judge in context.

questions.q: How do I make my distorted guitar warmer?
questions.short: Change the cabinet impulse and low-pass at 7–8 kHz. Warmth here is a speaker, not an EQ.
steps: Try a different cabinet impulse response first; it changes more than any EQ.
Low-pass at 7–8 kHz. A real guitar speaker rolls off here anyway.
Lift 1–2 dB at 200–400 Hz, but only if the bass allows it.
Reduce the gain; less distortion is warmer.
Add tube saturation after the amp rather than more amp gain.
questions.why: A guitar cabinet is a bandpass filter with a strong character, and amp sims that sound cold usually have a thin or over-bright impulse loaded. Changing it is the equivalent of changing the speaker, which is where guitar tone actually lives.
questions.watch: 200–400 Hz on guitars is the most crowded band in a band mix. Add warmth sparingly.

questions.q: How do I clean up my distorted guitar?
questions.short: Low-pass the fizz, high-pass the mud, and reduce the gain. Three moves, in that order.
steps: Low-pass at 7–9 kHz; everything above is amp-sim fizz.
High-pass at 100–120 Hz.
Cut 3 dB at 200–400 Hz for the gain buildup.
Reduce the amp gain before adding a fourth EQ move.
Gate the gaps if the amp hisses between parts.
questions.why: A distorted guitar occupies a much narrower useful band than it produces: nothing above about 7 kHz is from the speaker and nothing below 100 Hz belongs to it in a band mix. Filtering to that band removes most of the clutter in one step.
questions.watch: Low-passing below 6 kHz makes the guitar sound like it is behind a door.

questions.q: How do I push my distorted guitar further back?
questions.short: Cut 2–4 kHz, pan wider, and add a short room. Lowering them loses the wall.
steps: Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz where the vocal needs presence.
Pan the pair wider; centre-heavy guitars always feel close.
Add a short room reverb, 0.6–1 s, at 10–15%.
Roll off above 7 kHz.
Lower the fader last, by 1–2 dB.
questions.why: Guitars feel close because their 2–4 kHz content is right where the ear is most alert. Removing that band moves them back without reducing the energy that makes a guitar wall feel large.
questions.watch: Cutting 2–4 kHz too deeply makes the guitars sound like they are in another room while still being loud.

questions.q: How do I make my distorted guitar more aggressive?
questions.short: Less gain, more mid-range. Aggression is 800 Hz–2 kHz, which high gain scoops out.
steps: Reduce the amp gain by a third.
Lift 2–3 dB at 800 Hz–2 kHz — the band metal mixes usually scoop.
Tighten the low end: high-pass at 120 Hz and cut 300 Hz.
Use a transient designer to raise the pick attack.
Double-track and pan wide rather than adding more distortion.
questions.why: High gain compresses the signal and scoops the mids, which sounds heavy alone and disappears in a mix. The mid-range is what the ear reads as aggression, which is why less gain and more mids is consistently heavier in context.
questions.watch: Mid-range guitars feel harsh soloed. Judge them against the full band.

questions.q: How do I get my distorted guitar more upfront?
questions.short: Add 1–3 kHz and keep them dry. Reverb on distorted guitars pushes them back immediately.
steps: Lift 2 dB at 1–3 kHz for presence.
Remove or reduce the reverb; distorted guitars rarely need any.
Narrow the pair slightly; very wide guitars feel further away.
Reduce the gain so the pick attack survives.
Cut the same band on the keys or pads to make room.
questions.why: Distortion already supplies sustain and density, so what a guitar usually lacks when it sits back is attack and mid-range. Both live between 1 and 3 kHz, and neither is helped by reverb.
questions.watch: 1–3 kHz on guitars is where the vocal lives too. Check them together before committing.

questions.q: Why does my distorted guitar sound boxy?
questions.short: The cabinet impulse. Change it before you reach for EQ.
steps: Try three different cabinet impulses; this usually fixes it entirely.
If it persists, sweep 300–600 Hz and cut 3–4 dB.
Check the mic position in the impulse — on-axis at the cone edge is less boxy.
Reduce the gain; boxiness grows with distortion.
Add 2 dB at 2 kHz afterwards for definition.
questions.why: Boxiness in a guitar tone is a resonance of the modelled speaker and cabinet rather than of the playing. Swapping the impulse is the equivalent of swapping the cab, which solves at source what EQ can only mask.
questions.watch: Cutting 300–600 Hz too deeply leaves the guitar thin and fizzy.

questions.q: Why does my distorted guitar sound thin?
questions.short: The mids are scooped. Put 800 Hz–2 kHz back and lower the high-pass.
steps: Check the amp's mid control; a scooped tone is thin by design.
Lift 2–3 dB at 800 Hz–2 kHz.
Lower the high-pass to 90–100 Hz.
Double-track and pan rather than boosting low end on one track.
Check the bass is not occupying the guitar's low mids.
questions.why: The scooped-mid tone that sounds enormous in isolation has had exactly the band removed that makes a guitar audible in a band. The thinness is not a lack of low end, it is a hole in the middle.
questions.watch: Adding low end to a thin guitar puts it in the bass's way without fixing the thinness.

questions.q: Why does my distorted guitar disappear in the mix?
questions.short: Scooped mids plus too much gain. Both make a guitar sound big alone and vanish in a band.
steps: Reduce the gain by a third and listen in context.
Lift 2–3 dB at 800 Hz–2 kHz, the band that cuts through.
High-pass at 120 Hz so the energy is where it is audible.
Pan the pair wider so they are not competing with the centre.
Cut the same mid band on the keys or synths.
questions.why: High gain compresses the guitar into a constant wall with no dynamics and no mid-range, which is exactly the profile that gets masked. Less gain and more mids reverses both at once.
questions.watch: Guitars that cut through a mix almost always sound harsher soloed than scooped ones.

questions.q: Why does my distorted guitar sound dull?
questions.short: The low-pass is too low, or the cabinet impulse is dark. Check both before boosting.
steps: Raise the low-pass to 8–9 kHz if you set it lower.
Try a brighter cabinet impulse.
Lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz for pick definition, not above 6 kHz.
Check the compressor attack is not removing the pick.
Reduce gain; very high gain is dark as well as loose.
questions.why: A guitar's bite is at 2–4 kHz, not in the air band, because a speaker cannot reproduce above about 6 kHz. Boosting higher finds only amp-sim fizz, which sounds harsh without sounding bright.
questions.watch: Boosting above 6 kHz on a distorted guitar adds hiss rather than definition.

questions.q: How do I make my clean electric guitar warmer?
questions.short: Tube saturation and a roll-off above 8 kHz. A clean DI has no amp to warm it.
steps: Add tube saturation or a clean amp sim; a DI alone is always cold.
Roll off 2 dB above 8 kHz.
Lift 1.5 dB at 200–400 Hz for body.
Use the neck pickup tone if you can re-record.
Add a short room so the note decays into something.
questions.why: A guitar amp is an EQ and distortion device as much as an amplifier, and a clean DI bypasses all of it. What is missing is harmonic content, which saturation supplies and EQ cannot.
questions.watch: 200–400 Hz on a clean guitar competes with the vocal's chest range.

questions.q: How do I make my clean electric guitar brighter?
questions.short: Lift 3–6 kHz for the pick and add a shelf above 10 kHz. Clear the low mids first.
steps: Cut 2 dB at 200–400 Hz; brightness appears without boosting.
Lift 2 dB at 3–6 kHz for the pick attack.
Add a 1.5 dB shelf above 10 kHz for air.
Use a transient designer if the picking is soft.
Switch to the bridge pickup if you can re-record.
questions.why: Unlike a distorted guitar, a clean one has real content above 6 kHz, so a high shelf works here where it would only find fizz on a distorted track. The pick attack at 3–6 kHz is what carries the definition.
questions.watch: Brightening a clean guitar also raises string squeak and fret noise.

questions.q: How do I make my clean electric guitar wider?
questions.short: A stereo chorus or two takes. For ambient parts, two different delay times beats any widener.
steps: Record the part twice and pan opposite if the part allows.
Otherwise use a stereo chorus or tremolo with modest depth.
For ambient parts, use two delays with different times, one per side.
High-pass at 120 Hz so the width does not carry low end.
Check mono; chorus survives it, Haas-based widening does not.
questions.why: A clean guitar is a single point source with sustain, so width has to come from modulation or from two performances. Modulation changes the two channels differently over time, which survives mono summing far better than a fixed delay.
questions.watch: Heavy chorus makes a clean guitar sound dated unless that is the intention.

questions.q: How do I clean up my clean electric guitar?
questions.short: High-pass, gate the hum, and de-ess the pick noise. The amp hiss is usually the problem.
steps: High-pass at 100–150 Hz.
Gate or edit the gaps; single-coil hum is constant otherwise.
Notch 50 or 60 Hz and its harmonics if there is mains hum.
Use a de-esser at 3–5 kHz for harsh pick attacks.
Cut 200–400 Hz if it muddies against the keys.
questions.why: A clean guitar has no distortion to mask noise, so hum, hiss and pick attacks are all fully audible. Most cleanup is therefore noise removal rather than tonal work.
questions.watch: Gating a clean guitar with long sustain chops the decay. Use a long release.

questions.q: How do I get my clean electric guitar more upfront?
questions.short: Compress for consistency, add 2–4 kHz, and reduce the reverb.
steps: Compress at 3:1 with 3–4 dB so every note is equally present.
Lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz for the pick.
Reduce the reverb send; clean guitars are usually too wet.
Narrow it toward the centre for its featured sections.
Cut 2–4 kHz on the keys or pads to make room.
questions.why: A clean guitar varies enormously between a soft and a hard pick, so the quiet notes vanish while the loud ones poke out. Compression makes the part continuously present, which the ear reads as closeness.
questions.watch: Compressing a clean guitar hard removes the picking dynamics that carry a highlife or worship part.

questions.q: How do I make my clean electric guitar sound more natural?
questions.short: Add an amp and a room. A clean DI is accurate and sounds nothing like a guitar in a space.
steps: Run it through a clean amp sim or add tube saturation.
Add a short room reverb; a guitar always exists in a room.
Keep the picking dynamics — compress at 2–3 dB at most.
Leave the string and fret noise in.
Vary the tone slightly between sections rather than one static setting.
questions.why: A DI captures the pickup's electrical output with no speaker, no cabinet and no air, which is why it sounds correct and unreal. Supplying the missing harmonic colour and the missing room is what makes it sound like an instrument.
questions.watch: Too much amp or room makes a clean guitar indistinct. Keep both subtle.

questions.q: Why does my clean electric guitar sound harsh?
questions.short: The pick attack at 2–5 kHz. Use a de-esser there rather than a static cut.
steps: Put a de-esser at 3–5 kHz so only the hard picks are reduced.
Slow the compressor attack so it stops exposing the transient.
Low-pass at 10–12 kHz if the DI is very bright.
Try the neck pickup or a softer pick if you can re-record.
Add tube saturation, which rounds the attack rather than removing it.
questions.why: A clean guitar's harshness appears only on hard picks, so it is a dynamic problem rather than a tonal one. A static cut dulls every softly picked note to fix the handful that were struck hard.
questions.watch: Cutting 3–5 kHz statically removes the definition that makes a clean part audible.

questions.q: Why does my clean electric guitar sound dull?
questions.short: Neck pickup, tone control rolled off, or something brighter covering it. Check in that order.
steps: Check whether the guitar's tone control was rolled off during recording.
Mute the hats and keys; if it opens up, cut them instead.
Cut 200–400 Hz; brightness appears by contrast.
Lift 2 dB at 3–6 kHz for the pick.
Add a 1.5 dB shelf above 10 kHz last.
questions.why: Clean guitars occupy the same upper mid-range as hats, keys and vocal consonants, so dullness is frequently masking rather than a missing top end. Checking by muting takes seconds and prevents an unnecessary boost.
questions.watch: Boosting a dull clean guitar raises amp hiss and single-coil hum with it.

questions.q: Why does my clean electric guitar disappear in the mix?
questions.short: Keys and vocals share its band. Compress it, carve them, and give it a position.
steps: Compress at 3:1 with 3–4 dB; inconsistency is why it vanishes.
Cut 2 dB at 1–3 kHz on the keys and pads.
Pan it 30–50% off centre so it is not competing with the vocal.
Lift 2 dB at 3–5 kHz for the pick, which nothing else has.
Automate it up in the gaps between vocal phrases.
questions.why: A clean guitar has little low end and no distortion sustain, so it is the quietest and most dynamic thing competing for the mid-range. Compression and a distinct pan position give it the only two advantages available.
questions.watch: Raising a clean guitar to compete usually makes it harsh before it makes it audible.

questions.q: Why does my clean electric guitar sound boxy?
questions.short: The amp sim's cabinet, or a semi-hollow body resonance. Cut 300–600 Hz narrow.
steps: Sweep 300–600 Hz and cut 3–4 dB at the worst spot.
Try a different cabinet impulse if it is an amp sim.
On a semi-hollow guitar, the resonance is the instrument — cut less.
Add 2 dB at 3 kHz afterwards for definition.
Check the keys are not adding to the same band.
questions.why: Boxiness is a resonance in the low mids, which on a clean guitar comes either from the modelled cabinet or from a hollow body. Knowing which matters, because a hollow body's resonance is part of the instrument's character.
questions.watch: Cutting a semi-hollow's resonance too hard removes what makes it sound like that guitar.

questions.q: How do I make my acoustic guitar warmer?
questions.short: Lift 150–250 Hz and roll off above 10 kHz. Avoid 100 Hz, which is boom not warmth.
steps: Lift 1.5–2 dB at 150–250 Hz with a wide bell.
Roll off 2 dB above 10 kHz if the strings are very bright.
Add tape saturation rather than more low end.
Lower the high-pass to 80 Hz if the acoustic is the only instrument.
Reduce the 3–5 kHz pick lift if you added one.
questions.why: An acoustic's warmth is the body resonance around 150–250 Hz, while 100 Hz and below is the sound hole's boom. The two are an octave apart, which is why boosting low end usually makes an acoustic boomy rather than warm.
questions.watch: 150–250 Hz is the vocal's chest range. In a singer-songwriter mix they will fight.

questions.q: How do I clean up my acoustic guitar?
questions.short: High-pass, notch the body resonance, and de-ess the string squeak.
steps: High-pass at 80–100 Hz, or 120 Hz in a full band mix.
Sweep 100–200 Hz for the body resonance and cut 3–5 dB.
Cut 2–3 dB at 200–400 Hz for the boxiness.
De-ess at 4–8 kHz for string squeak and pick noise.
Edit out the loudest finger slides by hand.
questions.why: An acoustic has three predictable problems: the sound hole's boom, the body's box, and string noise. Each is narrow and in a known place, which is why three targeted moves work better than broad shaping.
questions.watch: De-essing an acoustic too hard removes the attack that makes strumming rhythmic.

questions.q: How do I make my acoustic guitar wider?
questions.short: Two mics or two takes. A stereo-recorded acoustic is already wide; a DI never will be.
steps: Record with two mics, one at the twelfth fret and one at the body, and pan them apart.
Or record the part twice and pan the takes opposite.
Check phase between the two mics before anything else.
High-pass both at 100 Hz so the width carries no low end.
Keep the low end centred even when the top is wide.
questions.why: Two mics at different positions capture genuinely different signals, which is real stereo. Widening a single mono acoustic with a plugin fabricates difference that cancels when summed.
questions.watch: Two mics on one acoustic will comb-filter if not phase-checked. Flip polarity and listen.

questions.q: How do I make my acoustic guitar sound more natural?
questions.short: Use a microphone rather than a pickup, keep the dynamics, and leave the string noise.
steps: Use a mic if you can; an under-saddle pickup never sounds natural alone.
If you only have a pickup, blend it with a mic or add a body impulse response.
Compress lightly, 3:1 and 2–3 dB. Strum dynamics are the part.
Leave string squeak and finger noise; removing them reads as synthetic.
Add a short room so it decays into a space.
questions.why: An under-saddle pickup senses string vibration at the bridge rather than the sound of the instrument in air, which is why it sounds quacky regardless of EQ. Blending a mic or a body impulse restores the missing resonance.
questions.watch: A fully natural acoustic can be hard to fit in a dense mix. Natural and audible sometimes conflict.

questions.q: How do I push my acoustic guitar further back?
questions.short: Cut 2–4 kHz, high-pass higher, and add reverb. The strum attack is what feels close.
steps: Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz where the strum attack and vocal consonants collide.
High-pass at 120–150 Hz in a full band.
Add a medium reverb, 1.2–1.8 s, at 15–25%.
Pan it 30–50% off centre.
Compress it so it stops peaking above the band.
questions.why: An acoustic's strum attack sits exactly where vocal consonants do, which both makes it feel close and makes it mask the vocal. Removing that band solves both at once.
questions.watch: In a sparse arrangement the acoustic is the rhythm section. Check before pushing it back.

questions.q: How do I get my acoustic guitar more upfront?
questions.short: Compress for consistency, lift 3–5 kHz, and reduce the reverb.
steps: Compress at 4:1 with 4–5 dB; strumming varies more than you think.
Lift 2 dB at 3–5 kHz for the pick and strum.
Reduce the reverb send; acoustics are usually over-wet.
Keep it near the centre for its featured sections.
Cut 3–5 kHz on the keys or hats to clear the band.
questions.why: An acoustic's level varies hugely between a soft fingerpick and a hard strum, so the quiet passages disappear while the loud ones are fine. Compression makes it continuously present, which reads as closeness.
questions.watch: Compressing an acoustic hard removes the strum dynamics that drive a sparse arrangement.

questions.q: How do I tighten up my acoustic guitar?
questions.short: Notch the body resonance and high-pass. The looseness is the sound hole, not the playing.
steps: Sweep 90–180 Hz for the body resonance and cut 4–5 dB narrow.
High-pass at 100–120 Hz.
Compress at 4:1 with 3–4 dB for consistency between strums.
Use a transient designer to reduce sustain if the ring is still long.
Edit out the longest open-string rings if they blur chord changes.
questions.why: The sound hole is a tuned port, so an acoustic has a strong resonance that rings far longer than the notes. Notching it tightens the instrument without touching the attack or the string detail.
questions.watch: Notching the body resonance out entirely makes the acoustic sound like a banjo.

questions.q: Why does my acoustic guitar sound harsh?
questions.short: Pick attack and string squeak at 3–6 kHz. De-ess rather than cutting statically.
steps: Put a de-esser at 4–7 kHz so only the harsh moments are reduced.
Sweep 2–5 kHz for a resonance and cut 3 dB if one jumps out.
Slow the compressor attack so it stops exposing the transient.
Move the mic away from the sound hole and toward the twelfth fret next time.
Use a softer pick or play nearer the neck if you can re-record.
questions.why: An acoustic's harshness appears only on hard strums and string slides, which makes it dynamic rather than tonal. De-essing targets exactly those moments and leaves the soft passages with their detail.
questions.watch: Static cuts at 4–6 kHz remove the strum definition that makes an acoustic rhythmic.

questions.q: Why does my acoustic guitar sound thin?
questions.short: Over-filtered, or an under-saddle pickup. Lower the high-pass and add a body impulse.
steps: Lower the high-pass to 80 Hz and listen again.
Lift 2 dB at 150–250 Hz for the body.
If it is a pickup, add a body impulse response or blend a mic.
Reduce the 200–400 Hz cut if you made one to clear mud.
Check the vocal is not occupying the acoustic's body range.
questions.why: An acoustic's body is 150–250 Hz, and the standard advice to high-pass at 120 Hz plus cut 300 Hz removes most of it. On a pickup there was never much there to begin with, which is why the two causes look identical.
questions.watch: Restoring the acoustic's body puts it directly in the vocal's chest range.

questions.q: Why does my acoustic guitar sound dull?
questions.short: Old strings, a mic at the sound hole, or something brighter covering it.
steps: Check the strings. Dead strings cannot be fixed in the mix.
Check the mic position — at the sound hole is boomy and dull.
Cut 200–400 Hz; brightness appears without boosting.
Add a 2 dB shelf above 8 kHz.
Mute the hats and cymbals to check whether it is masking.
questions.why: An acoustic's sparkle comes from the strings' upper harmonics, which dead strings simply do not produce. No amount of boosting creates harmonics the instrument did not make.
questions.watch: Boosting above 8 kHz on a dull acoustic raises hiss and room before it raises sparkle.

questions.q: Why does my acoustic guitar disappear in the mix?
questions.short: Keys and electrics share its whole range. Give it 3–6 kHz, which only it has.
steps: Lift 2 dB at 3–6 kHz for the strum, and cut the same band on the keys.
Compress at 4:1 with 4 dB for consistency.
Pan it 30–50% off centre.
High-pass at 120 Hz so its energy is where it is audible.
Automate it up in the sections where it carries the rhythm.
questions.why: An acoustic covers the same range as piano, clean guitar and vocal all at once, so there is no band it owns by default. Its strum transient at 3–6 kHz is the one thing none of those has, which makes it the only reliable place to claim.
questions.watch: Boosting 3–6 kHz also raises string squeak. De-ess after.

questions.q: How do I make my piano warmer?
questions.short: Lift 200–400 Hz and roll off above 10 kHz. Add tape before you add EQ.
steps: Add tape saturation before the EQ.
Lift 1.5 dB at 200–400 Hz with a wide bell.
Roll off 2 dB above 10 kHz if the sample is bright.
Reduce the hammer noise at 4–6 kHz if it is making it hard.
Use a softer velocity layer if it is a sampled piano.
questions.why: A piano's warmth is the body of its lower-mid notes plus the soundboard's resonance, both around 200–400 Hz. Sampled pianos are usually recorded bright and close, which captures the hammer and underplays the body.
questions.watch: 200–400 Hz on a piano collides with the vocal, the guitars and the snare simultaneously.

questions.q: How do I clean up my piano?
questions.short: High-pass by role, cut the low mids once, and narrow the stereo image.
steps: High-pass at 120–200 Hz in a full arrangement; let the bass own below.
Cut 2–3 dB at 250–400 Hz.
Narrow the width to 60–70% so it stops surrounding everything.
Check whether the left hand doubles the bass line.
Reduce the pedal if the sustain is blurring chord changes.
questions.why: A piano spans the entire range of every other instrument, so cleaning it is mostly about deciding which octaves it is allowed to occupy. That is a filtering and arrangement decision rather than a tonal one.
questions.watch: On a solo piano recording none of this applies. Filter only when something else needs the room.

questions.q: How do I make my piano wider?
questions.short: It probably already is. Most piano samples are recorded wide — the question is usually how to narrow it.
steps: Check the existing width before adding any; most piano libraries are already 100%.
If genuinely narrow, use mid/side to raise the sides 2 dB above 300 Hz.
Keep the low notes narrower than the high ones if the plugin allows.
Choose a player perspective and keep it consistent with the rest of the mix.
Check mono; wide piano often loses its centre entirely.
questions.why: Piano is one of the few sources that arrives already wide, because it was recorded with a stereo pair across a two-metre instrument. Widening it further usually produces a hole in the centre rather than more width.
questions.watch: A full-width piano competes with the vocal reverb for the sides and leaves the centre hollow.

questions.q: How do I make my piano sound more natural?
questions.short: Vary the velocities, keep the pedal and the sustain, and add a real room.
steps: Vary velocities; a sampled piano at one velocity switches between layers audibly.
Keep the pedal noise and the release samples if the library has them.
Add a room or hall reverb; a dry piano is never natural.
Compress lightly, 2–3 dB at most.
Check the sustain is not being cut short by a gate or a short release.
questions.why: A piano's realism lives in its sustain, its sympathetic resonance and the mechanical noise of the action. Sampled pianos include all three, and the usual tidying moves — gating, heavy compression, dry mixing — remove them.
questions.watch: Too much reverb on a piano makes it distant rather than natural. Keep it short.

questions.q: How do I make my piano sound bigger?
questions.short: A longer reverb and the full range. Size in piano is space plus the low octaves.
steps: Lower the high-pass so the left hand keeps its weight — but only if the bass allows.
Add a hall reverb, 1.8–2.6 s, with 25–40 ms pre-delay.
Widen to full and let it surround, if nothing else needs the sides.
Add a gentle lift at 80–150 Hz for the low octaves.
Thin the arrangement; a big piano needs room more than it needs EQ.
questions.why: A piano is physically large and its realism depends on that scale, so size comes from giving it back its full range and a room big enough for it. In a dense arrangement neither is available, which is the real constraint.
questions.watch: A big piano and a full band cannot both have the low mids. Decide which the song is about.

questions.q: How do I get my piano more upfront?
questions.short: Narrow it toward the centre, lift 2–4 kHz, and reduce the reverb.
steps: Narrow it to 50–60% and move it toward the centre.
Lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz for the hammer attack.
Reduce the reverb send; piano is usually the wettest thing in a mix.
Compress at 3:1 with 3 dB for consistency.
Cut the same band on the guitars or pads.
questions.why: Width and reverb both signal distance, and a piano usually has plenty of each by default. Narrowing and drying it is therefore more effective than any level change, and costs no headroom.
questions.watch: A narrow dry piano in a sparse arrangement can sound small rather than close.

questions.q: Why does my piano sound boxy?
questions.short: Close-miked soundboard resonance at 300–600 Hz. Cut it narrow and check the room.
steps: Sweep 300–600 Hz and cut 3–4 dB at the worst spot.
Check whether a different mic position in the sample library is available.
Reduce the close mics and raise the room mics if the library has both.
Add 2 dB at 3 kHz afterwards for definition.
Check the keys and guitars are not adding to the same band.
questions.why: A piano's soundboard resonates in the low mids, and close mics inside the lid capture that resonance far more strongly than a listener would hear it. Many sample libraries ship with mic position options, which is a better fix than EQ.
questions.watch: Cutting 300–600 Hz too hard leaves the piano sounding like a toy.

questions.q: Why does my piano sound harsh?
questions.short: Hammer noise at 2–5 kHz on the loud notes. Cut it dynamically, not statically.
steps: Dynamic EQ at 2–5 kHz cutting 3–4 dB on the loudest notes only.
Lower the velocity curve in the sampler so hard notes trigger a softer layer.
Slow the compressor attack.
Roll off above 12 kHz if the library is very bright.
Check the arrangement — a piano playing high and loud over a full band will always be harsh.
questions.why: A piano gets brighter the harder it is played, because the hammer strikes the string with more force and excites more upper partials. The harshness therefore exists only in the loud passages, which is what makes it a dynamic problem.
questions.watch: Dulling the piano statically removes the clarity of the quiet passages too.

questions.q: Why does my piano disappear in the mix?
questions.short: It spans everything, so everything masks part of it. Give it one octave to own.
steps: Decide which octave the piano owns and filter the rest of it out.
Lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz for the hammer, and cut that band on the guitars.
Narrow it so it is not spread thinly across the whole field.
Automate it up in the gaps between vocal phrases.
Thin the voicings; a piano playing full chords in a full band is mostly inaudible anyway.
questions.why: A piano overlaps every instrument in the arrangement because it covers the whole range, so it is masked a little by everything rather than a lot by one thing. Narrowing its range gives it somewhere it is the only occupant.
questions.watch: Raising a masked piano makes the mix denser without making the piano audible.

questions.q: Why does my piano sound dull?
questions.short: Low-mid buildup covering it, or a soft velocity layer. Cut 300 Hz before boosting.
steps: Cut 2 dB at 250–400 Hz; the brightness appears by contrast.
Check the velocities — soft layers on a sampled piano are much darker.
Add a 2 dB shelf above 8 kHz.
Lift 1 dB at 5 kHz for the hammer only if the attack is still soft.
Mute the hats and cymbals to check for masking.
questions.why: Sampled pianos switch between velocity layers recorded at different intensities, and the soft layers are genuinely darker because a softly struck string produces fewer upper partials. Raising the MIDI velocity changes the sample rather than just the level.
questions.watch: Boosting 1–3 kHz to brighten a piano makes it clangy rather than bright.

questions.q: Why does my piano sound thin?
questions.short: Over-filtered for a sparse arrangement. The 150 Hz high-pass that works in a band is wrong alone.
steps: Lower the high-pass to 60–80 Hz when the piano is exposed.
Automate the filter: high in the full sections, low in the sparse ones.
Lift 2 dB at 150–300 Hz for body.
Check the voicing; high closed voicings are thin regardless of EQ.
Widen it slightly in the sparse sections.
questions.why: A piano needs very different filtering depending on whether a bass is playing, and most mixes set one filter for the whole song. Automating it is the correct answer rather than compromising between the two.
questions.watch: Leaving the filter low through the full sections puts the piano straight back into the bass.

questions.q: How do I make my organ warmer?
questions.short: Tube saturation and a roll-off above 8 kHz. The warmth is the amp, not the drawbars.
steps: Add tube saturation or a Leslie emulation; a clean organ patch is always cold.
Roll off 2–3 dB above 8 kHz.
Add a slow rotor effect if there is none; movement reads as warmth.
Lift 1 dB at 200–400 Hz only if the mix has room.
Reduce the percussion drawbar if the attack is making it hard.
questions.why: A Hammond's sound is inseparable from its valve amplifier and rotating speaker, both of which add harmonic distortion and movement. A straight organ patch has the drawbars without the circuit, which is exactly what sounds cold.
questions.watch: An organ already fills the low mids. Adding 300 Hz there compounds quickly.

questions.q: How do I clean up my organ?
questions.short: High-pass at 200 Hz, cut 300–500 Hz, and narrow it. An organ fills every gap by design.
steps: High-pass at 180–250 Hz. Much higher than feels right, and it works.
Cut 3 dB at 300–500 Hz where it collides with voices and guitars.
Narrow it to 60–70% so it stops surrounding the listener.
Duck it 2 dB under the lead vocal.
Reduce the number of drawbars out rather than EQing the result.
questions.why: A Hammond with drawbars out produces sustained harmonics across the entire spectrum with no gaps, which is its function in an arrangement. Everything else must be given space by removing organ, because the organ never stops.
questions.watch: Filtering above 250 Hz removes the pedal bass that anchors a traditional arrangement.

questions.q: How do I make my organ wider?
questions.short: Use the Leslie's top rotor in stereo. Keep the bass rotor mono and centred.
steps: Mic or emulate the horn rotor in stereo and pan the pair 70–100% out.
Keep the bass rotor mono and centred; it is too slow for a useful image.
Use the rotor speed change rather than a widener for movement.
High-pass the stereo portion at 300 Hz.
Check mono; the Doppler effect survives it, a widener does not.
questions.why: A Leslie's width comes from two microphones hearing the horn's Doppler sweep at different moments, which is genuine channel difference. The bass rotor turns too slowly to produce that, which is why widening it only causes phase problems.
questions.watch: A wide organ eats the whole stereo field. Narrow it rather than widening it in most mixes.

questions.q: How do I make my organ sound bigger?
questions.short: Drawbars and the Leslie, not EQ. An organ's size is in the registration and the rotor.
steps: Pull more drawbars out rather than boosting frequencies.
Use the Leslie's fast rotor for excitement and slow for size.
Add tube saturation; an overdriven Hammond is the sound of a big organ.
Widen the horn rotor pair.
Thin the arrangement; a big organ needs room more than it needs level.
questions.why: A Hammond's registration is additive synthesis — each drawbar is a harmonic — so the size of the sound is chosen at the instrument rather than shaped afterwards. EQ can only emphasise harmonics that a drawbar already produced.
questions.watch: A big organ in a full gospel arrangement leaves no room for the choir. That is a decision, not a fault.

questions.q: How do I smooth out my organ?
questions.short: Compress gently and ride the swell pedal in automation. The organist's dynamics are the part.
steps: Compress at 3:1 with 2–3 dB only; heavier flattens the Leslie's own swell.
Automate the level to follow what the swell pedal should have done.
Cut 2–3 dB at 300–500 Hz so loud passages do not become muddy as well as loud.
Use a slow attack so the percussion drawbar survives.
Ride it down under the vocal rather than compressing it there.
questions.why: The Leslie's rotation produces its own amplitude modulation, and compression fights that directly. Automating the level instead leaves the rotor's movement intact while controlling the section-to-section dynamics.
questions.watch: Compressing a Leslie flattens the rotor swell, which is the entire effect.

questions.q: Why does my organ disappear in the mix?
questions.short: It is usually the opposite problem. If it really is buried, give it 1–3 kHz with the rotor moving.
steps: Check first that it is actually buried and not just correctly placed.
Add a brighter drawbar registration rather than EQ.
Use the fast rotor; movement makes a sustained part audible without level.
Lift 2 dB at 1–3 kHz and cut the same band on the guitars.
Automate it up in the turnarounds where it should lead.
questions.why: A sustained source with no transient is hard to pick out of a mix, which is why movement does more for an organ than level. The rotating speaker creates continuous change that the ear tracks even at a low level.
questions.watch: In most gospel mixes the organ is too loud rather than too quiet. Check before raising it.

questions.q: Why does my organ sound harsh?
questions.short: Upper drawbars plus distortion. Pull the drawbars in before you reach for EQ.
steps: Pull in the upper drawbars; that is the harshness at source.
Reduce the overdrive on the Leslie emulation.
Cut 3–4 dB at 2–5 kHz with a dynamic EQ.
Roll off above 8 kHz.
Check the horn rotor mics are not too close in the emulation.
questions.why: A Hammond's upper drawbars are discrete harmonics, so harshness from them sits at specific frequencies rather than across a band. Removing the drawbar is exact where EQ is approximate.
questions.watch: Dulling the organ too far removes the bite that lets it cut through a full band.

questions.q: Why does my organ sound boomy?
questions.short: The pedal bass is doubling the bass guitar. Decide which one owns the bottom.
steps: Check whether the organ pedals and the bass are playing the same notes.
If so, high-pass the organ at 200 Hz and let the bass have it.
If the pedals are the bass, high-pass the bass guitar instead.
Notch any single resonant note between 60 and 150 Hz.
Keep the organ's low end mono.
questions.why: Organ pedals and a bass guitar in the same octave produce slow beating rather than a clean sum, because the two will never be perfectly in tune with each other. This is an arrangement decision, and EQ can only pick a winner.
questions.watch: In traditional gospel the organ pedal often is the bass. Removing it leaves a hole.

questions.q: Why does my organ sound dull?
questions.short: Not enough upper drawbars, or no percussion. Fix the registration before the EQ.
steps: Pull out more upper drawbars.
Add the percussion drawbar for attack on each key press.
Use the fast rotor; it reads as brighter as well as more energetic.
Only then lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz.
Check the low-pass on the Leslie emulation is not set too low.
questions.why: A Hammond generates its tone from discrete drawbars, so if a harmonic is not pulled out it is not in the signal. EQ can only amplify what the registration already produced, which is why the fix is at the instrument.
questions.watch: Boosting an organ's top end without the drawbars raises the Leslie's amp noise.

questions.q: How do I make my Rhodes brighter?
questions.short: Lift 1–3 kHz for the tine and add a phaser. Brightness here is the bell, not the air.
steps: Lift 2 dB at 1–3 kHz for the tine attack.
Add a slow phaser or chorus; movement reads as brightness.
Cut 200–400 Hz to let the top through.
Increase the velocity if it is a sampled Rhodes; harder strikes are brighter.
Add a 1 dB shelf above 8 kHz last, if at all.
questions.why: A Rhodes produces its characteristic bell from the tine striking at 1–3 kHz, and it has very little content above 6 kHz. Boosting an air band on a Rhodes therefore finds mostly noise.
questions.watch: 1–3 kHz on a Rhodes is also the vocal's intelligibility band. Check them together.

questions.q: How do I clean up my Rhodes?
questions.short: High-pass at 120 Hz, cut 250–400 Hz, and reduce the chorus depth.
steps: High-pass at 120–150 Hz; the bass owns below.
Cut 2–3 dB at 250–400 Hz.
Reduce the chorus or tremolo depth if it is smearing the notes.
Shorten the release if chords are overlapping.
Gate the hum if it is a real instrument with pickup noise.
questions.why: A Rhodes is a sustained mid-range source with a lot of low-mid energy, so clutter is usually overlap rather than noise. Filtering and shortening the overlap does more than any detailed EQ.
questions.watch: Filtering a Rhodes above 200 Hz removes the body that distinguishes it from a synth pad.

questions.q: How do I make my Rhodes wider?
questions.short: Stereo tremolo or chorus. The instrument's own vibrato is already a stereo effect.
steps: Use the Rhodes' own stereo tremolo; that is what it was built with.
Add a stereo chorus at modest depth if the tremolo is not enough.
Keep everything below 200 Hz mono.
Pan the dry signal slightly off centre and let the modulation do the rest.
Check mono; tremolo survives it, a widener does not.
questions.why: A real Rhodes has a stereo tremolo that pans the signal between channels, which is genuine channel difference over time rather than phase manipulation. It therefore survives mono summing as a level change rather than a cancellation.
questions.watch: Fast tremolo plus a stereo chorus becomes seasick very quickly.

questions.q: How do I push my Rhodes further back?
questions.short: Cut 1–3 kHz, add a longer reverb, and widen it. The tine attack is what feels close.
steps: Cut 2 dB at 1–3 kHz, the tine band that also carries the vocal.
Add a medium reverb, 1.4–2 s, at 18–25%.
Widen it; wide and wet reads as further away for a sustained source.
Roll off above 7 kHz.
Lower the fader last.
questions.why: A Rhodes' only transient is its tine attack, so removing that band is the single most effective way to move it back. Unlike a percussive source, widening it also pushes it back rather than forward, because it has no attack to anchor.
questions.watch: Cutting the tine entirely leaves the Rhodes sounding like a pad.

questions.q: How do I make my Rhodes sound more natural?
questions.short: Vary the velocity, add the amp and the tremolo, and keep the key noise.
steps: Vary velocities; a Rhodes changes timbre dramatically with how hard it is played.
Add an amp sim or tube saturation; a Rhodes always went through an amp.
Use the instrument's own tremolo rather than a plugin chorus.
Keep the key and tine noise if the library includes it.
Compress lightly, 2–3 dB at most.
questions.why: A Rhodes' bark at high velocity and bell at low velocity are completely different timbres, so a part played at one velocity sounds synthetic however good the samples. Velocity variation is more important here than on almost any other keyboard.
questions.watch: Over-compressing a Rhodes removes the velocity differences you just created.

questions.q: Why does my Rhodes sound muddy?
questions.short: Low voicings plus a long sustain. Filter at 150 Hz and shorten the release.
steps: High-pass at 120–180 Hz.
Cut 2–3 dB at 250–400 Hz.
Shorten the release so chords stop overlapping.
Check the voicings; low closed voicings on a Rhodes are mud by definition.
Reduce the chorus depth, which smears the low mids.
questions.why: A Rhodes sustains for several seconds, so overlapping chords accumulate low-mid energy that never clears. Shortening the release addresses the accumulation; filtering addresses what is left.
questions.watch: Low voicings are often the arrangement's intent. Ask before filtering them out.

questions.q: Why does my Rhodes sound dull?
questions.short: Low velocity. A Rhodes played softly is genuinely dark — raise the velocity, not the EQ.
steps: Raise the MIDI velocity; this changes the sample, not just the level.
Lift 2 dB at 1–3 kHz for the tine.
Cut 250–400 Hz so the top comes through by contrast.
Check the amp sim's tone control is not rolled off.
Add a phaser for movement rather than more treble.
questions.why: A Rhodes tine struck softly produces almost no upper harmonics, which is a physical property of the instrument rather than a recording limitation. Velocity is the tone control, and EQ cannot add harmonics the tine never made.
questions.watch: Raising velocity also raises level. Compensate on the channel so you are comparing fairly.

questions.q: Why does my Rhodes sound harsh?
questions.short: High velocity bark at 2–4 kHz. Lower the velocity or cut that band dynamically.
steps: Lower the MIDI velocity on the loudest notes; the bark is a velocity layer.
Dynamic EQ at 2–4 kHz cutting 3 dB on the hardest notes.
Reduce the amp sim's drive.
Roll off above 8 kHz.
Slow the compressor attack.
questions.why: A hard-struck Rhodes tine produces a characteristic bark, which is an intentional part of the instrument's range rather than a fault. It only becomes harsh when it appears on every note, which is a velocity problem.
questions.watch: Removing the bark entirely leaves a Rhodes with no dynamic expression at all.

questions.q: Why does my Rhodes sound thin?
questions.short: Over-filtered, or a bell-heavy patch. Lower the high-pass and add 200–400 Hz.
steps: Lower the high-pass to 100–120 Hz.
Lift 2 dB at 200–400 Hz for body.
Choose a warmer patch or a lower velocity layer.
Add tube saturation rather than more EQ.
Check the bass is not occupying the Rhodes' body range.
questions.why: A Rhodes' body is 200–400 Hz, the same band usually cut to clear mud, so the standard cleanup makes it thin. Because it is a sustained source, that band is also where it is most likely to be in the way — which is the tension.
questions.watch: Restoring the Rhodes' body puts it directly against the vocal's chest and the guitars.

questions.q: How do I make my synth lead brighter?
questions.short: Open the filter at the synth. EQ is the second choice when you can change the instrument.
steps: Raise the filter cutoff at the synth before anything else.
Add a filter envelope so the attack is brighter than the sustain.
Only then lift 2 dB at 3–6 kHz.
Add a 1.5 dB shelf above 10 kHz if the patch has content there.
Turn on oversampling if you are adding saturation.
questions.why: A synth's filter is a brightness control with far more range and better behaviour than any mixing EQ, and it changes the harmonic content rather than just the balance. Using EQ first is working around a control that is already available.
questions.watch: Opening the filter also raises resonance artefacts. Check the loudest notes.

questions.q: How do I clean up my synth lead?
questions.short: Reduce the unison, high-pass at 200 Hz, and low-pass the aliasing above 12 kHz.
steps: Reduce unison voices; eight detuned saws is mud, not width.
High-pass at 150–250 Hz.
Low-pass at 12–14 kHz to remove digital content no speaker needs.
Turn on oversampling for any distortion in the chain.
Shorten the release if notes are overlapping.
questions.why: A synth lead's clutter is usually generated rather than captured: too many unison voices, aliasing from distortion, and content above the audible range. All three are fixed at the source rather than with EQ.
questions.watch: Reducing unison narrows the lead. Pan it or add a chorus if you need the width back.

questions.q: How do I get my synth lead more upfront?
questions.short: Narrow it to the centre, add 2–4 kHz, and reduce the reverb.
steps: Narrow it toward the centre; wide synths always feel further away.
Lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz.
Reduce the reverb; a dry lead is a close lead.
Compress at 3:1 with 3 dB so it is consistently present.
Duck the pads and keys 2 dB under it.
questions.why: A synth lead is usually wide and wet by default because the preset was designed to sound impressive in isolation. Both of those cues signal distance, which is why the preset that sounded huge alone sits at the back in a mix.
questions.watch: 2–4 kHz on a synth lead collides directly with the vocal. Decide which one leads.

questions.q: How do I make my synth lead more aggressive?
questions.short: Filter resonance, a fast envelope and distortion with oversampling on.
steps: Raise the filter resonance and add a fast filter envelope.
Add distortion with oversampling enabled.
Shorten the amplitude attack to zero.
Lift 2 dB at 1.5–3 kHz.
Narrow it; wide synths feel soft.
questions.why: Aggression is a hard attack plus upper-harmonic density, both of which a synth can generate at the source far more convincingly than a plugin can add afterwards. Oversampling matters because aggressive distortion is exactly when aliasing appears.
questions.watch: Aliasing from distortion sounds harsh rather than aggressive, and it gets worse on low notes.

questions.q: How do I push my synth lead further back?
questions.short: Widen it, darken it, and add a delay. Wide and dark reads as distant for a sustained source.
steps: Widen it; a wide sustained source feels further away.
Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz where the vocal lives.
Roll off above 8 kHz.
Add a stereo delay rather than reverb so it stays defined.
Duck it 2–3 dB under the lead vocal.
questions.why: For a source with no transient, width and darkness both read as distance — the opposite of a percussive source, where width can bring things forward. That makes widening a useful way to move a synth back without lowering it.
questions.watch: Widening a synth lead too far makes it collapse on a phone where the hook needs to be heard.

questions.q: How do I make my synth lead sound bigger?
questions.short: Detuned unison plus an octave layer, not reverb. Size here is harmonic density.
steps: Use two or three detuned unison voices, 8–15 cents apart.
Add an oscillator an octave below, filtered so it does not reach the sub.
Keep everything below 150 Hz mono.
Add a stereo delay rather than a long reverb.
Pan the unison voices rather than using a widener.
questions.why: A synth lead's size comes from the number of slightly different oscillators sounding at once, which is why detuned unison works where reverb only adds distance. The octave layer gives the ear a second pitch reference, which reads as weight.
questions.watch: Too much unison makes a lead sound out of tune against a piano or horns.

questions.q: Why does my synth lead sound thin?
questions.short: A single oscillator with the filter open. Add unison and a lower octave.
steps: Add a second detuned oscillator, 8–12 cents apart.
Add an octave below, filtered at 150 Hz so it stays out of the bass.
Lower the high-pass to 120 Hz.
Lift 2 dB at 200–500 Hz for body.
Add saturation for harmonic density rather than EQ.
questions.why: A single oscillator produces a mathematically exact waveform with no beating, which the ear hears as thin regardless of its frequency content. Density comes from several slightly different sources, not from EQ.
questions.watch: Adding a lower octave puts the lead into the bass's range. Filter it.

questions.q: Why does my synth lead disappear in the mix?
questions.short: It is in the vocal's band. Move it in pitch, in time or in position — not in level.
steps: Check whether it plays at the same time as the vocal; if so, that is the fix.
Move it up or down an octave to a range nothing else occupies.
Narrow it so it is a point source rather than a spread.
Add a filter envelope; movement makes a sustained part audible.
Automate it up in the gaps between vocal phrases.
questions.why: A synth lead and a vocal are both sustained mid-range melodies, so they mask each other almost completely when they overlap. Arrangement — different octave or different moment — solves what no amount of EQ can.
questions.watch: Raising a masked synth lead over a vocal is the quickest way to an unintelligible chorus.

questions.q: Why does my synth lead sound dull?
questions.short: The filter is closed. Open it at the synth before touching EQ.
steps: Raise the filter cutoff at the synth.
Add a filter envelope so the attack is brighter than the sustain.
Check for a low-pass later in the chain that you forgot.
Lift 2 dB at 3–6 kHz only after the above.
Add a brighter oscillator waveform — saw rather than triangle.
questions.why: A synth's filter removes harmonics at the source, so EQ afterwards is boosting a band that has already been emptied. Opening the filter restores the content rather than amplifying its absence.
questions.watch: Opening the filter can introduce aliasing on high notes. Check the top of the range.

questions.q: Why does my synth lead sound muddy?
questions.short: Too many unison voices and no high-pass. Reduce the voices before you cut anything.
steps: Reduce unison to two or three voices.
High-pass at 200–250 Hz.
Cut 2–3 dB at 250–400 Hz.
Shorten the release so notes stop overlapping.
Reduce the sub oscillator if the patch has one.
questions.why: Each unison voice adds a full copy of the waveform's low-mid content, so eight voices produce eight times the mud of one. Because they are detuned, that energy also beats against itself, which no EQ can separate.
questions.watch: Reducing unison narrows the lead. Use panning or chorus to recover the width.

questions.q: How do I make my pad wider?
questions.short: It probably already is. Pads are usually too wide rather than too narrow.
steps: Check the existing width first; most pad presets are already 100%.
If genuinely narrow, use detuned unison panned apart rather than a widener.
Keep everything below 200 Hz mono.
Use a stereo chorus or a slow modulated delay for movement.
Check mono; a pad that vanishes there is cancelling, not widening.
questions.why: Pad presets are designed to sound impressive alone, which means maximum width by default. In a mix that width occupies the sides where the vocal reverb and the guitars need to be, which is why narrowing is the more common requirement.
questions.watch: A very wide pad plus a wide reverb leaves no clean sides for anything else.

questions.q: How do I clean up my pad?
questions.short: Filter both ends hard. A pad only needs the middle, and everything else is in the way.
steps: High-pass at 250–350 Hz and low-pass at 8–10 kHz.
Cut 2–3 dB at 300–500 Hz on top of the filter.
Reduce the number of layers in the patch rather than EQing the sum.
Shorten the release if chords are overlapping.
Mono everything below 200 Hz.
questions.why: A pad's job is to fill space without being noticed, which means it only needs a narrow band. Everything outside that band is energy that competes with sources the listener is supposed to hear.
questions.watch: Filtering both ends too hard leaves a pad sounding like a telephone.

questions.q: How do I make my pad warmer?
questions.short: Lower the filter at the synth and add tape. Resist adding low mids — a pad has enough.
steps: Lower the filter cutoff at the synth.
Add tape saturation for even harmonics.
Roll off above 8 kHz rather than boosting low mids.
Add slow movement — a slow LFO on the filter reads as warmth.
Use a chamber reverb rather than a plate.
questions.why: A pad already has more low-mid energy than almost anything else in a mix because it sustains, so the usual warming move of boosting 300 Hz immediately produces mud. Removing top end achieves the same perception without adding anything.
questions.watch: Warming a pad with low mids is the single most common cause of a continuously muddy mix.

questions.q: How do I make my pad sound bigger?
questions.short: A long reverb and slow movement, not more level or more layers.
steps: Add a hall reverb, 2.5–4 s, with a long pre-delay.
Add a slow LFO on the filter so the pad never quite settles.
Detune two layers slightly for beating.
Widen it, if the sides are free.
Keep the level low; a big pad does not have to be loud.
questions.why: A pad is the one source that can take a very long reverb without smearing anything, because it has no transients to blur. That makes reverb the cheapest route to size here, where on any other source it would cost clarity.
questions.watch: A long pad reverb fills the gaps the drums need. High-pass the return hard.

questions.q: How do I smooth out my pad?
questions.short: Lengthen the attack and release at the synth, and compress very gently.
steps: Lengthen the amplitude attack to 200–500 ms so chords fade in.
Lengthen the release so chords overlap smoothly.
Compress at 2:1 with 1–2 dB only.
Reduce any filter envelope so the timbre does not change abruptly.
Automate the level between sections rather than compressing harder.
questions.why: A pad's unevenness is almost always its envelope rather than its dynamics, because every note is triggered at the same velocity. Lengthening the attack and release at the synth smooths the thing that is actually jumping.
questions.watch: Very long attacks make the pad arrive after the chord change. Check against the harmony.

questions.q: Why does my pad disappear in the mix?
questions.short: That is usually correct. Mute it — if the mix feels empty, the pad is working.
steps: Mute it. If the mix shrinks noticeably, the pad is doing its job.
If nothing changes, raise it 2 dB and widen it.
Add slow filter movement so the ear notices it without more level.
Give it a frequency band nothing else occupies, usually 500 Hz–3 kHz.
If it still does nothing, the arrangement does not need it.
questions.why: A pad is designed to be felt rather than heard, so not noticing it is the intended outcome. The mute test is the only reliable way to tell a working pad from an unnecessary one.
questions.watch: Raising a pad until it is clearly audible usually makes the mix muddy rather than fuller.

questions.q: Why does my pad sound harsh?
questions.short: Filter resonance or aliasing. Lower the resonance and low-pass at 9 kHz.
steps: Lower the filter resonance at the synth.
Low-pass at 8–10 kHz; a pad needs nothing above that.
Cut 3 dB at 2–5 kHz where the vocal needs room anyway.
Turn on oversampling for any saturation in the chain.
Choose a warmer waveform — triangle or sine layers rather than saws.
questions.why: A pad sustains, so any harshness is continuous rather than momentary and becomes fatiguing much faster than the same peak on a transient source. That is why pads need more aggressive top-end filtering than their level suggests.
questions.watch: A pad is the easiest thing to darken because nobody is listening to it directly. Use that.

questions.q: Why does my pad sound lifeless?
questions.short: Nothing is moving. A pad without modulation is a sustained chord, not a texture.
steps: Add a slow LFO on the filter cutoff, one cycle every four to eight bars.
Detune two layers so they beat slowly against each other.
Automate the filter opening across a section.
Add a slow chorus or a modulated delay.
Vary the voicing between sections rather than holding one chord.
questions.why: The ear stops registering anything that does not change, so a static pad becomes inaudible within seconds regardless of its level. Slow modulation keeps it just above the threshold of attention, which is where a pad belongs.
questions.watch: Fast modulation draws attention to the pad, which is the opposite of its job.

questions.q: Why does my pad sound phasey?
questions.short: A stereo widener or extreme unison spread. Remove it and mono the low end.
steps: Remove any stereo widener from the pad.
Reduce the unison stereo spread at the synth.
Mono everything below 200 Hz.
Use a chorus for movement instead; it modulates rather than cancels.
Fold to mono and listen for the pad thinning.
questions.why: Pad presets often reach their width with a Haas delay or a polarity trick, both of which cancel when summed. Because a pad sustains, that cancellation is continuous rather than momentary and is very audible in mono.
questions.watch: A pad that vanishes in mono was never adding what you thought it was adding.

questions.q: How do I make my strings warmer?
questions.short: Use a warmer articulation, add a hall, and roll off the bow noise.
steps: Choose a warmer articulation in the sampler before touching EQ.
Add a hall reverb; dry strings are always cold.
Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz for the bow noise.
Lift 1 dB at 200–400 Hz for body if the mix has room.
Add tape saturation for harmonic density.
questions.why: Real strings are almost always heard in a hall, where the room absorbs the bow noise before it reaches the listener. A dry sampled string section is an instrument nobody has ever encountered, which is why it sounds cold by default.
questions.watch: Too much hall makes strings distant rather than warm. Keep the pre-delay short.

questions.q: How do I make my strings brighter?
questions.short: Choose a brighter articulation and add a shelf above 10 kHz. Avoid 2–5 kHz.
steps: Try a more intense articulation or a higher dynamic layer in the sampler.
Add a 2 dB shelf above 10 kHz for rosin and air.
Cut 200–400 Hz; brightness appears by contrast.
Leave 2–5 kHz alone; that is bow noise, not brightness.
Raise the close mics relative to the hall mics if the library has both.
questions.why: String brightness that reads as beautiful is the rosin and air above 10 kHz, while 2–5 kHz is bow scrape. Boosting the lower band makes strings sound screechy rather than bright, which is why the shelf has to go high.
questions.watch: Boosting above 10 kHz on a sampled library raises the recording's noise floor too.

questions.q: How do I clean up my strings?
questions.short: High-pass the violins, keep the cellos low, and cut the bow noise once on the bus.
steps: High-pass the violins and violas at 200–300 Hz; let the cellos keep their bottom.
Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz on the bus for bow noise.
Cut 2 dB at 250–400 Hz if the section is muddy.
Split the parts rather than filtering one wide patch.
Compress the bus lightly, 2–3 dB, so the section breathes together.
questions.why: A string ensemble patch contains violins and cellos at once, so a single high-pass either leaves the violins muddy or removes the cellos. Splitting the parts is what makes targeted filtering possible.
questions.watch: High-passing a full string patch at 300 Hz removes the cellos entirely.

questions.q: How do I push my strings further back?
questions.short: More hall, less close mic, and cut 2–4 kHz. Strings belong behind almost everything.
steps: Raise the hall mics and lower the close mics if the library has both.
Add more hall reverb, 2.5–3.5 s, at 25–35%.
Cut 2–3 dB at 2–4 kHz where the vocal lives.
Roll off above 10 kHz.
Lower the fader last.
questions.why: Strings in an orchestra sit well behind the soloist, and sampled libraries' close mics put them in front instead. Favouring the hall mics restores the relationship the ear expects without changing the balance.
questions.watch: Very wet strings lose their articulation. Keep enough close mic for the attacks.

questions.q: How do I make my strings sound bigger?
questions.short: Split the parts, pan them as an orchestra sits, and share one long hall.
steps: Split into separate violin, viola and cello parts.
Pan them as they sit in a real section: high strings left, low strings right.
Use one hall reverb, 2.5–3.5 s, across the whole group.
Vary each part's timing by a few milliseconds so they are not locked.
Add an octave-doubled violin line if the arrangement allows.
questions.why: A string section's size comes from many players spread across a stage in one shared hall, which a single stereo patch cannot reproduce. Splitting, placing and sharing one reverb rebuilds that arrangement.
questions.watch: Separate reverbs on each part make them sound like separate recordings.

questions.q: How do I make my strings sound more natural?
questions.short: Vary the dynamics, use legato articulations, and put everything in one hall.
steps: Automate the dynamics continuously; real strings never hold a steady level.
Use legato and portamento articulations rather than separate note triggers.
Offset each part's timing by a few milliseconds.
Use one hall reverb across the whole section.
Avoid perfectly quantised entries; a section does not arrive at the same instant.
questions.why: Real string players swell and taper continuously and never enter perfectly together, which is why static sampled strings sound synthetic even with excellent samples. The dynamics automation is the single biggest factor.
questions.watch: Dynamics automation on strings changes the sample layer as well as the level, which is the point.

questions.q: How do I smooth out my strings?
questions.short: Compress the bus gently and automate the dynamics. The jumps are usually layer switches.
steps: Automate the dynamics control smoothly rather than in steps.
Compress the bus at 2:1 with 2–3 dB.
Use dynamic EQ at 2–5 kHz so loud passages do not also get harsher.
Check for abrupt sample-layer changes at the dynamics crossover points.
Lengthen the reverb so the transitions are covered.
questions.why: A sampled library switches between dynamic layers recorded at different intensities, so a sudden dynamics change swaps timbre as well as level. Smooth automation keeps the crossfade gradual enough to be inaudible.
questions.watch: Compressing strings hard flattens the swells that make them expressive.

questions.q: Why do my strings sound thin?
questions.short: No cellos. A string arrangement without a low part is thin regardless of EQ.
steps: Check the arrangement — are there cellos and basses, or only violins?
Add a cello line an octave or two below the violins.
Lower the high-pass to 150 Hz on the low parts.
Lift 1–2 dB at 200–400 Hz on the whole section.
Add a hall reverb; dry strings always sound thinner.
questions.why: A string section's weight comes from its lowest instruments, so an arrangement of only violins has no foundation whatever is done to it in the mix. This is an arrangement problem wearing a mixing problem's clothes.
questions.watch: Boosting low end on violins produces mud without body. Add a low part instead.

questions.q: Why do my strings sound muddy?
questions.short: Low voicings plus sustain. Split the parts and filter the high ones properly.
steps: Split the patch into separate parts so you can filter each by range.
High-pass the violins at 250–300 Hz.
Cut 2–3 dB at 250–400 Hz on the bus.
Check the voicings; close low voicings on strings are mud by nature.
Reduce the reverb's low end — a hall tail is muddy too.
questions.why: Strings sustain continuously, so their low-mid content never clears the way a transient source's does. Combined with low close voicings, they become one of the most reliable causes of a mix that is muddy throughout.
questions.watch: Filtering a combined string patch removes the cellos. Split first.

questions.q: Why do my strings disappear in the mix?
questions.short: They are a sustained mid-range source, which is the most crowded position in any mix.
steps: Give them an octave nothing else occupies, usually above the vocal.
Add movement — a swell or a moving line is audible where a held chord is not.
Lift 2 dB at 5–8 kHz for the rosin, which nothing else has.
Narrow them slightly so they are not spread thin.
Automate them up in the gaps between vocal phrases.
questions.why: Sustained mid-range sources have no transient for the ear to latch onto, so they are masked more easily than anything else. Movement and a distinctive high band are the two things that make them audible without more level.
questions.watch: Raising buried strings usually muddies the mix before it makes them audible.

questions.q: Why do my strings sound dull?
questions.short: Low dynamics layer, or too much hall mic. Raise both before reaching for EQ.
steps: Raise the dynamics automation; soft layers are genuinely darker.
Raise the close mics relative to the hall mics.
Cut 250–400 Hz; brightness appears by contrast.
Add a 2 dB shelf above 10 kHz.
Check for a low-pass you forgot on the bus.
questions.why: String dynamics layers are recorded at genuinely different bow intensities, so a quietly played passage has fewer upper harmonics rather than just less level. The dynamics control is the tone control.
questions.watch: Raising the dynamics also raises the level. Compensate before judging.

questions.q: How do I make my horns brighter?
questions.short: Lift 4–8 kHz and clear the low mids. Brass brightness is the bell, not the air.
steps: Cut 2 dB at 200–400 Hz; brightness appears by contrast.
Lift 2 dB at 4–8 kHz for the bell's edge.
Raise the dynamics if it is a sampled library; loud brass is brighter.
Add a touch of saturation rather than more EQ.
Leave above 12 kHz alone; brass has little content there.
questions.why: Brass gets brighter as it gets louder because the air column distorts, pushing energy into the upper harmonics. That brightness lives at 4–8 kHz rather than in an air band, which is why a high shelf does little for horns.
questions.watch: Brightening horns is one step from making them harsh. Use dynamic EQ if it only hurts on the stabs.

questions.q: How do I make my horns warmer?
questions.short: Add a room, cut 2–5 kHz dynamically, and lift 200–500 Hz.
steps: Add a room or hall reverb; dry brass is always harsh.
Dynamic EQ at 2–5 kHz cutting on the loudest stabs only.
Lift 1–2 dB at 200–500 Hz for the body of the instrument.
Add tape saturation rather than more EQ.
Use a softer articulation or lower dynamics layer if sampled.
questions.why: Brass is almost never heard dry in real life, so the room is part of what the ear expects. Adding it does more for perceived warmth than any EQ move, because it supplies the absorption that softens the upper harmonics naturally.
questions.watch: 200–500 Hz on horns collides with vocals and guitars. Add warmth sparingly in a full band.

questions.q: How do I clean up my horns?
questions.short: High-pass at 150 Hz, cut the bus once at 2–5 kHz, and gate the breath between stabs.
steps: High-pass at 150–200 Hz; horns need no low end under a band.
Dynamic EQ at 2–5 kHz on the bus for the stabs.
Gate or edit the gaps; breath and key noise between stabs is constant otherwise.
Cut 2 dB at 400–700 Hz if the section is honky.
Process on the bus, not per horn.
questions.why: Horns play in bursts, so most of their channel time is breath, key noise and bleed. Editing the gaps removes a disproportionate amount of the clutter without touching the stabs.
questions.watch: Gating horns too tightly cuts the attack of the stab, which is the whole point of the part.

questions.q: How do I make my horns wider?
questions.short: Pan the players as they would stand. A section is several mono sources, not one wide one.
steps: Pan each horn to its own position: trumpets wider, trombone and sax nearer centre.
If it is one stereo patch, split it into separate parts and pan those.
Use one shared room reverb, panned wide, rather than widening the sources.
Keep the lowest horn nearest the centre.
Check mono; real panning survives, a widener does not.
questions.why: A horn section is several separate instruments standing apart, so its width is genuine spatial separation rather than stereo processing. Panning the parts reproduces that; widening a summed patch only exaggerates a recording's existing image.
questions.watch: Hard-panning a three-piece section leaves a hole in the middle where the lead horn should be.

questions.q: How do I get my horns more upfront?
questions.short: Compress the bus, lift 2–4 kHz, and reduce the reverb for the stabs.
steps: Compress the bus at 4:1 with 4–6 dB so every stab lands the same size.
Lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz for the bite.
Reduce the reverb send during the stabs and raise it after.
Narrow them toward the centre for featured lines.
Automate the whole bus up for the stabs.
questions.why: Horn stabs vary enormously between players and takes, so the quiet ones vanish while the loud ones poke out. Compression plus automation puts every stab at the same perceived level, which is what makes a section sound tight and present.
questions.watch: 2–4 kHz on horns is also where they turn harsh. Use dynamic EQ alongside the boost.

questions.q: How do I make my horns more aggressive?
questions.short: Raise the dynamics layer, compress hard, and add saturation. Loud brass is aggressive brass.
steps: Use the loudest dynamics layer or articulation; brass distorts as it gets louder.
Compress the bus at 6:1 with 5–8 dB.
Add tube saturation after the compressor.
Raise attack on a transient designer for the stab.
Keep them dry; reverb softens aggression.
questions.why: A brass instrument played hard genuinely distorts, which is why the aggressive sound is a different recording rather than a processed version of a soft one. Saturation imitates the same mechanism when the library has no louder layer.
questions.watch: Aggressive horns are a step from painful. Dynamic EQ at 2–5 kHz keeps them the right side.

questions.q: How do I make my horns sound more natural?
questions.short: Vary the dynamics continuously, offset the players' timing, and put them in one room.
steps: Automate dynamics continuously; brass swells on every note.
Offset each horn's timing by a few milliseconds so they do not enter together.
Add breath and key noise if the library has it.
Use one room reverb across the section.
Avoid perfectly quantised stabs; a real section is never exact.
questions.why: A real horn section never enters at the same instant or holds a steady level, and sampled brass is unconvincing mostly because it does both. Timing offsets and continuous dynamics fix more than any amount of EQ.
questions.watch: Too much timing offset turns a section into a flam. Keep it under 20 ms.

questions.q: Why do my horns sound boxy?
questions.short: A peak at 400–800 Hz, from close miking or a small recording room.
steps: Sweep 400–800 Hz and cut 3–4 dB at the worst spot.
Cut once on the bus; every horn shares the resonance.
Raise the room mics if the library has them.
Add 2 dB at 3 kHz afterwards for the bite.
Move the mic further back and off-axis next session.
questions.why: A brass instrument's bell is highly directional and very loud, so a close mic captures the bore's resonance along with the note. Backing off and going off-axis reduces it at the source, which is where the real fix lives.
questions.watch: Cutting 400–800 Hz too deeply leaves horns thin and reedy.

questions.q: Why do my horns sound thin?
questions.short: No trombone or baritone. A section of trumpets and alto is thin by arrangement.
steps: Check the arrangement; a section needs a low voice.
Add a trombone or baritone sax line below the trumpets.
Lower the high-pass to 120 Hz on the low horns.
Lift 1–2 dB at 200–500 Hz on the bus.
Add a room reverb; dry horns sound thinner than they are.
questions.why: A horn section's weight comes from its lowest instrument, so an arrangement without one is thin regardless of processing. Boosting low end on trumpets adds mud rather than body because the content is not there.
questions.watch: Adding a low horn puts the section into the bass and guitars' range. Filter it.

questions.q: Why do my horns disappear in the mix?
questions.short: They play in bursts, so a static balance cannot serve both the stabs and the pads.
steps: Automate the section up for the stabs and down between them.
Compress the bus so every stab lands the same size.
Lift 2 dB at 2–4 kHz, and cut that band on the guitars.
Pan them away from whatever is in the same range.
Check whether the stabs land on the vocal; if so, move one of them.
questions.why: Horns appear for a few beats at a time, so the level that suits their sustained passages is far too quiet for their stabs. This is an automation problem that looks like a balance problem.
questions.watch: Raising horns globally makes the breath and bleed between stabs audible.

questions.q: Why do my horns sound dull?
questions.short: Soft dynamics layer, or the mic was off-axis. Raise the dynamics before the EQ.
steps: Raise the dynamics automation; soft brass is genuinely darker.
Raise the close mics relative to the room mics.
Cut 200–400 Hz; the bite appears by contrast.
Lift 2 dB at 4–8 kHz.
Check for a low-pass left on the bus.
questions.why: Brass timbre changes dramatically with playing intensity because the air column distorts more as it is driven harder. A soft layer simply does not contain the upper harmonics, so EQ has nothing to amplify.
questions.watch: Raising the dynamics also makes the horns louder and harsher. Compensate and check 2–5 kHz.

questions.q: How do I glue my mix together on the bus?
questions.short: One compressor, 1.5:1 to 2:1, 1–3 dB, slow attack, release timed to the tempo. Mix into it.
steps: Insert it at the start of the mix and leave it there; do not add it at the end.
Ratio 1.5:1 or 2:1, attack 30 ms, release timed to the tempo.
Aim for 1–3 dB of gain reduction at the loudest point.
High-pass the sidechain at 80–120 Hz so the kick stops driving it.
Bypass it occasionally; if the mix falls apart, it is doing too much.
questions.why: A single compressor across everything makes every source duck when any one of them peaks, and that shared movement is what the ear reads as one record rather than many tracks. Adding it late invalidates every balance decision made underneath it.
questions.watch: More than 3 dB on a mix bus is shaping rather than gluing, and it will pump.

questions.q: How do I clean up my mix?
questions.short: Work on the channels, not the bus. A cluttered mix is an arrangement with too much in one band.
steps: High-pass everything that is not kick, bass or 808, by ear not by default.
Find the three sources crowding 200–400 Hz and cut the worst one.
Mute each element in turn and leave muted whatever you do not miss.
Pan more aggressively; clutter is often everything in the centre.
Only then consider a bus cut, and keep it under 1 dB.
questions.why: Clutter is cumulative across sources, so no single bus move can address it without dulling everything. Finding the two or three real contributors treats the cause, and muting treats it best of all.
questions.watch: Cutting on the bus to clean a mix removes the same band from the things that needed it.

questions.q: How do I make my mix warmer?
questions.short: Tape saturation on the bus and a 1 dB lift at 150–300 Hz. Small moves, because they apply to everything.
steps: Add tape or console saturation on the mix bus, driven until you can just hear it.
Lift 1 dB at 150–300 Hz with a very wide bell.
Roll off 1 dB above 12 kHz if the mix is brittle.
Check the low mids are not already crowded before boosting them.
Compare at matched loudness; saturation adds level and flatters.
questions.why: On a mix bus every move applies to every source at once, so a 1 dB lift is the equivalent of a 1 dB lift on forty channels. That is why bus moves are a tenth the size of channel moves and still audible.
questions.watch: Warmth added on the bus compounds with every channel's own low mids. Check for mud after.

questions.q: How do I make my mix brighter?
questions.short: A 1 dB shelf above 10 kHz, after clearing the low mids. Brightness is a ratio.
steps: Cut 1 dB at 200–400 Hz first; the mix brightens with no boost at all.
Add a 1–1.5 dB shelf above 10 kHz.
Check whether one dark source is dragging the whole mix down.
Use saturation rather than EQ if the mix sounds dull and quiet.
Check your monitoring level and your ears before deciding the mix is dull.
