questions.why: Perceived brightness is the ratio between top and low mids, so clearing the low mids raises it without adding any energy. That matters on a bus, where every dB of boost costs headroom across the whole mix.
questions.watch: A mix that sounds dull after two hours is ear fatigue. Take a break before touching the bus.

questions.q: How do I make my mix sound bigger?
questions.short: Take things away. A big mix is one with space in it, not one with everything turned up.
steps: Mute something. Space is what makes the remaining elements sound large.
Give the important elements more contrast: dry against wet, narrow against wide.
Extend the low end on the kick and bass rather than everything.
Add width to the sides only, 1–2 dB above 300 Hz.
Check the arrangement before touching the bus at all.
questions.why: Size is relative, so it is created by contrast rather than by level. A mix where everything is loud, wide and full has no reference points, which is why it sounds smaller than one with deliberate space.
questions.watch: Bus processing almost never makes a mix bigger. Arrangement and contrast do.

questions.q: How do I make my mix sound more natural?
questions.short: Less of everything. Fewer plugins, less compression, and real dynamics between sections.
steps: Reduce the total compression on every channel by a third and listen.
Keep the verse genuinely quieter than the chorus.
Use one shared room reverb rather than six different spaces.
Remove any plugin you cannot justify when you bypass it.
Limit 2–3 dB rather than 6.
questions.why: What reads as processed is the absence of variation: in level between sections, in dynamics within a performance, and in space between sources. Every one of those is removed by a standard mixing move, which is why restraint is the technique.
questions.watch: A natural mix will measure quieter. That is the trade, and streaming normalisation makes it a fair one.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound muddy?
questions.short: Six sources each with a little 200–400 Hz add up to one unusable mix.
steps: High-pass everything that is not kick, bass or 808. Start at 100 Hz and move by ear.
Find the single worst offender in 200–400 Hz and cut that one, not all of them.
Check the organ, the pads and the reverb returns first; they fill that range continuously.
High-pass every reverb return at 300 Hz.
Only then touch the mix bus, and only by a decibel.
questions.why: Mud is cumulative. Nothing sounds wrong in solo because each source contributes only a decibel or two, which is exactly why cutting on the mix bus treats the symptom and dulls everything else with it.
questions.watch: If the mix goes thin after high-passing, you went too high on the instruments carrying the warmth.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound lifeless?
questions.short: Everything is at the same level all the time. Lifeless is a dynamics problem, not a tonal one.
steps: Check the crest factor; under 5 dB means the mix is squashed.
Reduce compression on the channels and the bus.
Make the verses genuinely quieter than the choruses.
Automate: nothing should sit at one level for three minutes.
Un-quantise the drums and percussion if they are perfectly on the grid.
questions.why: Energy in music is change over time, and every standard mixing move reduces change: compression removes dynamics, quantising removes timing variation, and static balance removes section contrast. Applied together they produce a mix that is controlled and dead.
questions.watch: Adding excitement with saturation or top end does not restore dynamics. Fix the cause.

questions.q: Why does everything in my mix fight everything else?
questions.short: Too many sources in one band. This is an arrangement problem, and the fix is subtraction.
steps: List every source and the band it occupies. The overlaps are your answer.
For each band, decide which source owns it and filter the others.
Mute each element in turn; whatever you do not miss stays muted.
Pan more aggressively — space is a dimension you may not be using.
Automate parts out of sections rather than leaving everything playing.
questions.why: A mix has a fixed amount of spectral and spatial room, and no amount of processing creates more. When everything fights, the arrangement has asked for more space than exists, which only removal or redistribution can solve.
questions.watch: Carving every source to make room for every other leaves a mix that is clean and empty.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound phasey?
questions.short: Find the source that vanishes in mono. It is almost always a widener or a Haas trick.
steps: Fold to mono and solo each source to find what disappears.
Remove any stereo widener, starting with the mix bus.
Check multi-mic sources for polarity: drums, guitars, DI plus amp.
Check for duplicated-and-delayed tracks.
Mono everything below 120 Hz.
questions.why: Phase problems do not accumulate evenly — one source is usually responsible. Soloing in mono finds it in minutes, where trying to fix the sum on the bus cannot work at all.
questions.watch: A mix can measure fine on a correlation meter and still lose a specific element in mono.

questions.q: Why does my mix sound boxy?
questions.short: Several sources sharing a room resonance at 300–600 Hz. Find them rather than cutting the bus.
steps: Sweep 300–600 Hz on the bus to find the frequency, then find which sources have it.
Cut it on the two or three worst sources rather than on the bus.
Suspect anything recorded in the same room: drums, vocal, guitars.
If four or more sources share it, cut 1 dB on the bus as well.
Check your own room; the boxiness may be where you are sitting.
questions.why: Boxiness across a whole mix usually means several sources were recorded in the same untreated room and all carry its resonance. Treating the sources removes it once each; treating the bus removes it from everything including the parts that were clean.
questions.watch: If the boxiness disappears on headphones, it is your listening room and not the mix.
